idiom_name: IO (File, TCPSocket) plus the block form of open
implementation_notes: Ruby's core classes are the wrapper facades: IO wraps a file descriptor, File is its only core subclass and TCPSocket/UDPSocket follow the same shape, and the block form (File.open { |io| ... }) gives the acquire/release pairing that a finalizer would otherwise have to guess. For a domain abstraction, subclass or wrap those types rather than calling the C API, and reserve a hand-written binding for a C library Ruby has no binding for (see the Fiddle variant).
pitfalls: ObjectSpace finalizers run on a background thread and at unpredictable times: a wrapper that closes only in a finalizer can lose buffered data at exit.
Ruby's IO buffers writes, so a facade that never flushes or closes hides data that never reached the operating system.
The GVL limits true parallelism: a facade over a blocking native call stalls other Ruby threads unless that call releases the GVL.

variants.name: Fiddle or ffi binding class
variants.idiom_name: Fiddle::Importer dlload/extern plus a Ruby class owning the handle
variants.implementation_notes: The standard library's Fiddle (a libffi wrapper) loads the shared object and binds the C functions as Ruby methods via dlload/extern or Fiddle::Function; the ffi gem offers the same with a richer DSL, struct support and GC of native memory. The facade is a class that stores the returned pointer, exposes intent-named methods and calls the library's destroy function in close(), with Fiddle.last_error consulted right after a failed call.
variants.code_sketch:
require 'fiddle/import'

module SensorLib
  extend Fiddle::Importer
  dlload 'libsensor.so'
  extern 'void* sensor_open(const char*)'
  extern 'void  sensor_close(void*)'
end

class Sensor
  def initialize(path) = @h = SensorLib.sensor_open(path)
  def close = (SensorLib.sensor_close(@h) if @h)
end
pitfalls: The handle returned by dlopen must outlive every bound function: letting the Fiddle::Handle be collected makes later calls dangle.
Fiddle::Function#call is not thread-safe by default, and passing need_gvl: true is what lets Ruby's C-extension APIs be called safely - the wrong choice deadlocks or corrupts.
Pointer arithmetic and struct layouts are the caller's responsibility: a type mismatch is a segmentation fault, not an exception.
